\chapter{Communication Complexity — Comparison}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from TCSlib.CommunicationComplexity.NewmanTheorem.Comparison
\section{Overview}

This module establishes comparison results between the three main communication
complexity models — deterministic, public-coin, and private-coin — by constructing
explicit comap-based protocol conversions.  The key result is that private-coin
communication complexity is bounded above by deterministic communication complexity
for any non-negative error parameter.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Public-coin protocol fixed to deterministic]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.Protocol.toDeterministic}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.Protocol.toDeterministic}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.comap, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.Protocol}
Given a public-coin protocol $p$ over randomness space $\Omega$ and a fixed
outcome $\omega : \Omega$, \texttt{PublicCoin.Protocol.toDeterministic}~$p~\omega$
is the deterministic protocol obtained by substituting $\omega$ for the shared
randomness (implemented via \texttt{comap} with $\mathrm{Prod.mk}\,\omega$).
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Fixing the shared randomness agrees with the randomised run]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.Protocol.toDeterministic_run}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.Protocol.toDeterministic_run}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.run, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.Protocol.rrun, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.Protocol.toDeterministic}
\difficulty{1}
Let $p$ be a public-coin protocol over a randomness space $\Omega$, with Alice's private
input in $X$, Bob's in $Y$, and output in $\alpha$, and fix a random outcome $\omega \in
\Omega$. For all private inputs $x \in X$ and $y \in Y$, executing the deterministic
protocol obtained from $p$ by fixing the shared randomness to $\omega$ on the pair $(x,
y)$ returns the same output in $\alpha$ as the randomised execution of $p$ on $x$ and
$y$ with shared random string $\omega$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Fixing shared randomness preserves communication complexity]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.Protocol.toDeterministic_complexity}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.Protocol.toDeterministic_complexity}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.complexity, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.Protocol.toDeterministic}
\difficulty{1}
Let $p$ be a public-coin communication protocol over a shared randomness space $\Omega$,
with Alice's private input in $X$, Bob's in $Y$, and output in $\alpha$, and let $\omega
\in \Omega$ be any outcome of the shared randomness. Then the communication complexity
of the deterministic protocol obtained from $p$ by fixing the shared randomness to
$\omega$ equals the communication complexity of $p$ itself.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Deterministic finite-message protocol to private-coin]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.toPrivateCoin}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.toPrivateCoin}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.comap, CommunicationComplexity.PrivateCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol}
Given a deterministic finite-message protocol $p$, the operation
\texttt{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.toPrivateCoin} converts it into a
private-coin finite-message protocol over arbitrary coin spaces $\Omega_X$ and
$\Omega_Y$ by ignoring both coin inputs (via \texttt{comap} with $\mathrm{Prod.snd}$).
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Ignoring private coins recovers the deterministic output]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.toPrivateCoin_rrun}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.toPrivateCoin_rrun}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.comap_run, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.run, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.toPrivateCoin, CommunicationComplexity.PrivateCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.rrun}
\difficulty{1}
Let $p$ be a deterministic finite-message protocol over input types $X$ and $Y$ with
output type $\alpha$, and fix arbitrary private-coin spaces $\Omega_X$ and $\Omega_Y$.
Form from $p$ the private-coin protocol over $\Omega_X$, $\Omega_Y$ that runs $p$ on the
underlying inputs while discarding both players' coins. Then for all inputs $x \in X$,
$y \in Y$ and all coin draws $\omega_x \in \Omega_X$, $\omega_y \in \Omega_Y$, executing
this private-coin protocol on $x$, $y$ with the coins $\omega_x$, $\omega_y$ returns
exactly the value that the deterministic execution of $p$ on $x$, $y$ produces,
regardless of the coins.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Complexity is preserved by passage to the private-coin model]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.toPrivateCoin_complexity}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.toPrivateCoin_complexity}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.complexity, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.toPrivateCoin}
\difficulty{1}
Let $p$ be a deterministic finite-message protocol over input types $X$, $Y$ and output
type $\alpha$, and let $\Omega_X$, $\Omega_Y$ be arbitrary types to serve as
private-randomness spaces. Form the private-coin finite-message protocol over
$\Omega_X$, $\Omega_Y$ obtained from $p$ by having each player ignore their private
coin, so that Alice's message function $f : X \to \beta$ is replaced by $(\omega, x)
\mapsto f(x)$ and Bob's by $(\omega, y) \mapsto f(y)$, with the protocol tree otherwise
unchanged. Then this private-coin protocol has the same communication complexity as $p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Public-coin finite-message protocol fixed to deterministic]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.toDeterministic}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.toDeterministic}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.comap, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol}
Given a public-coin finite-message protocol $p$ and a fixed randomness sample
$\omega : \Omega$, \texttt{PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.toDeterministic}~$p~\omega$
is the deterministic finite-message protocol obtained by substituting $\omega$
for the shared randomness (via \texttt{comap} with $\mathrm{Prod.mk}\,\omega$).
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Fixing randomness commutes with execution]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.toDeterministic_run}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.toDeterministic_run}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.comap_run, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.run, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.rrun, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.toDeterministic}
\difficulty{1}
Let $p$ be a public-coin finite-message protocol over a shared-randomness space
$\Omega$, private input sets $X$ and $Y$, and output type $\alpha$. Fix a randomness
sample $\omega \in \Omega$ and private inputs $x \in X$ and $y \in Y$, and let
$p_\omega$ denote the deterministic finite-message protocol obtained from $p$ by
substituting $\omega$ for the shared randomness. Then executing $p_\omega$ on $x$ and
$y$ yields the same output as the randomized execution of $p$ on $x$ and $y$ with shared
randomness $\omega$:
\[
p_\omega.\mathrm{run}(x, y) \;=\; \mathrm{rrun}(p, x, y, \omega).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Fixing shared randomness preserves communication complexity]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.toDeterministic_complexity}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.toDeterministic_complexity}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.complexity, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.toDeterministic}
\difficulty{1}
Let $p$ be a public-coin finite-message protocol over a shared-randomness space
$\Omega$, private input sets $X$ and $Y$, and output type $\alpha$, and let $\omega \in
\Omega$ be any fixed randomness sample. Then the deterministic finite-message protocol
obtained by substituting $\omega$ for the shared randomness has the same communication
complexity as $p$ itself.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Private-coin complexity at most deterministic complexity]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.PrivateCoin.communicationComplexity_le_deterministic}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.PrivateCoin.communicationComplexity_le_deterministic}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.CoinTape, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.comap_run, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.ofProtocol_equiv, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.run, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.toPrivateCoin, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.communicationComplexity, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.communicationComplexity_le_iff, CommunicationComplexity.PrivateCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.rrun, CommunicationComplexity.PrivateCoin.communicationComplexity, CommunicationComplexity.PrivateCoin.communicationComplexity_le_iff_finiteMessage}
\difficulty{4}
Let $f : X \times Y \to \alpha$ be a function of two arguments, and let $\varepsilon \ge
0$ be an error parameter. Then the $\varepsilon$-error private-coin randomized
communication complexity of $f$ is at most its deterministic communication complexity:
\[
  R_\varepsilon(f) \;\le\; D(f),
\]
as an inequality of extended natural numbers.
\end{theorem}
